advisories.title: Potential path transversal exposure in HlsSegmentController.cs
advisories.summary:
### Impact

The request path in HlsSegmentController is not validated to a valid path and could allow escaping the transcode path and downloading of any arbitrary file in GetHlsPlaylistLegacy .

GetHlsAudioSegmentLegacy and GetHlsVideoSegmentLegacy have the same issue, and are NOT behind an Authorize so they are publicly exploitable.

advisories.title: Potential IDOR in playlist management
advisories.summary:
### Impact

The `/Playlists/{playlistId}/Items` endpoint accepts a `userId` query parameter and uses it as the "calling user" for authorization purposes without verifying that the authenticated caller is allowed to act as that user. As a result, any authenticated non-admin user can read the items of another user's private playlist by adding `?userId=<victim-guid>` to the URL. This can result in information disclosure of private data from one user to another.

### Patches
Fixed in v12.0 via improved authentication checks on the affected endpoint.

### Workarounds
N/A

### References

PoC and report provided by Jeffry Mozalbat (@jeffry55).

advisories.title: Broken access control in session remote-control API
advisories.summary:
### Impact
AssertCanControl in SessionManager.cs only null-checks its arguments. It never verifies session ownership or the EnableRemoteControlOfOtherUsers permission. All the session remote-control endpoints are bare [Authorize], so any authenticated user who knows a target session ID can send popups, control playback, and issue system commands to another user's client. Session IDs are MD5(clientName + deviceId), so they can be computed offline rather than stolen.

advisories.title: Path traversal in the virtual-folder management endpoints allows deletion and relocation of arbitrary directories
advisories.summary:
### Impact
DELETE /Library/VirtualFolders and POST /Library/VirtualFolders/Name concatenate the caller-supplied library name onto the user-views root without validation, then pass the result to Directory.Delete(path, true) or Directory.Move. Because Path.Combine accepts a rooted second argument, the name escapes the library root either way:

- name=.. → <data>/root, name=../.. → <data>
- name=/var/lib/jellyfin/data → the root is discarded entirely

This lets an attacker recursively delete or relocate any directory the server process can write, including the data directory and jellyfin.db. Impact is permanent data loss and denial of service.

Before the startup wizard is completed, the FirstTimeSetupOrElevated policy grants anonymous access, so a freshly installed server reachable on the network can be destroyed without credentials. That is the primary risk. After setup, the endpoints require an administrator, who can already delete libraries - that variant is hardening only.

POST /Library/VirtualFolders (add) is not affected; it sanitizes the name through IFileSystem.GetValidFilename.

### Patches
_Has the problem been patched? What versions should users upgrade to?_

### Workarounds
- Complete the setup wizard immediately after installation, and keep a new server off untrusted networks until then - that is the unauthenticated window.
- Block /Library/VirtualFolders at a reverse proxy until setup is complete.
- Run the server as an unprivileged account limited to its own data and media directories.
- Keep backups of the data directory.

advisories.title: Memory exhaustion and SSRF via external references in user-supplied SVG images
advisories.summary:
### Impact
Jellyfin rasterizes SVG images server-side through Svg.Skia (SkiaEncoder.GetBitmapFromSvg and SkiaEncoder.GetImageSize). The SVG parser is invoked with library defaults, which resolve external references in <image xlink:href="...">. A crafted SVG therefore causes the server to read arbitrary local paths and fetch arbitrary URLs while rendering. This has two consequences.

1. Denial of service through memory exhaustion. A reference to an endless or very large file such as file:///dev/urandom is read into memory without a size limit. The read fails silently: no exception is raised, the render produces a transparent image, and the allocated memory is retained by the managed heap rather than returned. Measured against an 8 GiB limit, a 16x16 SVG produced a 4.1 GiB peak working set with 3.8 GiB still held after the load completed; under a 1.5 GiB limit it consumed 970 MiB. The consumption scales to the memory available to the process. Because the stored SVG is re-rasterized on subsequent image requests, a single upload provides a repeatable trigger without re-uploading.

2. Server-side request forgery and local file disclosure. http:// and https:// references are fetched by the server. Since a resized SVG is rasterized into the requested output format, the fetched response is rendered into an image the requester can then download - responses that decode as an image can be exfiltrated, not merely triggered. file:// references likewise expose local files that decode as an image.

Both are reachable by:

- Any authenticated user, by setting a profile image (POST /UserImage). SVG is an accepted image type for user images.
- Library import, where an administrator is induced to import media accompanied by a crafted poster.svg. The local image providers pick up .svg artwork. This path requires an administrator, but the administrator need not author the file.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential XSS in user management
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Prior to 10.11.9, a potential XSS attack exists in Jellyfin which can allow a non-privileged user to execute arbitrary Javascript in the context of a logged-in Administrative user, resulting in numerous potential issues. The Client header during an AuthenticateByName can contain arbitrary HTML and Javascript, which will then be executed by the Administrative user when visiting the Access tab of the user in question from within the dashboard. This vulnerability is fixed in 10.11.9.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential MKV attachment filename path traversal to RCE
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Prior to 10.11.10, a specifically crafted MKV file containing forged filename tags can be leveraged to exploit missing path sanitization during playback. Jellyfin treats the MKV file name tag on MKV attachments as trusted and passes it unsanitized into Path.Combine(attachmentFolder, fileName) inside PathManager.GetAttachmentPath. Because .NET's Path.Combine neither normalises .. nor rejects a rooted second argument, a crafted MKV can redirect Jellyfin's MKV attachment extraction to any absolute path on disk. This triggers on any playback action of the affected video on a client which will attempt to burn in the subtitles by default.g This vulnerability is fixed in 10.11.10.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential Authenticated path traversal in /ClientLog/Document
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. From 10.9.0 until 10.11.10, the POST /ClientLog/Document endpoint accepts the Authorization header's Client and Version fields and uses them unsanitized as components of the on-disk filename when persisting client-uploaded log documents. As a result, any authenticated non-admin user can include ../ sequences in the Client field to cause Jellyfin to write attacker-controlled content to arbitrary paths reachable by the Jellyfin service user, with a forced .log suffix. This vulnerability is fixed in 10.11.10.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential FFmpeg argument injection via unescaped subtitle file path
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Prior to 10.11.10, a potential FFmpeg argument injection vulnerability exists in the subtitle conversion code path. SubtitleEncoder.ConvertTextSubtitleToSrtInternal (SubtitleEncoder.cs, line 382) interpolates the subtitle file path into FFmpeg command-line arguments without calling EncodingUtils.NormalizePath(). On Linux, filenames can contain double-quote characters, which break the argument quoting and allow injection of arbitrary FFmpeg arguments. The vulnerability is reachable without authentication via SubtitleController.GetSubtitle, which has no [Authorize] attribute. An attacker who can place a file in a Jellyfin media library directory (shared NAS, Samba share, guest upload) can achieve arbitrary file write on the server and information disclosure. This vulnerability is fixed in 10.11.10.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential SSRF + Arbitrary file read via stream argument injection
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Versions prior to 10.11.7 contain an unauthenticated arbitrary file read vulnerability via ffmpeg argument injection through the StreamOptions query parameter parsing mechanism. The ParseStreamOptions method in StreamingHelpers.cs adds any lowercase query parameter to a dictionary without validation, bypassing the RegularExpression attribute on the level controller parameter, and the unsanitized value is concatenated directly into the ffmpeg command line. By injecting a drawtext filter with a textfile argument, an attacker can read arbitrary server files such as /etc/shadow and exfiltrate their contents as text rendered in the video stream response. The vulnerable /Videos/{itemId}/stream endpoint has no Authorize attribute, making this exploitable without authentication, though item GUIDs are pseudorandom and require an authenticated user to obtain. This issue has been fixed in version 10.11.7.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential Application DoS from excessively large SyncPlay group names
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Versions prior to 10.11.7 contain a denial of service vulnerability in the SyncPlay group creation endpoint (POST /SyncPlay/New), where an authenticated user can create groups with names of unlimited size due to insufficient input validation. By sending large payloads combined with arbitrary group IDs, an attacker can lock out the endpoint for other clients attempting to join SyncPlay groups and significantly increase the memory usage of the Jellyfin process, potentially leading to an out-of-memory crash. This issue has been fixed in version 10.11.7.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential SSRF + Arbitrary file read via LiveTV M3U tuner
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Versions prior to 10.11.7 contain a vulnerability chain in the LiveTV M3U tuner endpoint (POST /LiveTv/TunerHosts), where the tuner URL is not validated, allowing local file read via non-HTTP paths and Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF) via HTTP URLs. This is exploitable by any authenticated user because the EnableLiveTvManagement permission defaults to true for all new users. An attacker can chain these vulnerabilities by adding an M3U tuner pointing to an attacker-controlled server, serving a crafted M3U with a channel pointing to the Jellyfin database, exfiltrating the database to extract admin session tokens, and escalating to admin privileges. This issue has been fixed in version 10.11.7. If users are unable to upgrade immediately, they can disable Live TV Management privileges for all users.

advisories.title: Jellyfin: Potential RCE via subtitle upload path traversal + .strm chain
advisories.summary: Jellyfin is an open source self hosted media server. Versions prior to 10.11.7 contain a vulnerability chain in the subtitle upload endpoint (POST /Videos/{itemId}/Subtitles), where the Format field is not validated, allowing path traversal via the file extension and enabling arbitrary file write. This arbitrary file write can be chained into arbitrary file read via .strm files, database extraction, admin privilege escalation, and ultimately remote code execution as root via ld.so.preload. Exploitation requires an administrator account or a user that has been explicitly granted the "Upload Subtitles" permission. This issue has been fixed in version 10.11.7. If users are unable to upgrade immediately, they can grant non-administrator users Subtitle upload permissions to reduce attack surface.

advisories.title: Resource Exhaustion DoS via Branding Endpoint
advisories.summary:
### Impact
@whoopsi-daisy has reported a potential DoS vulnerability in Jellyfin. The Branding API endpoint allows an unauthenticated user to request a custom splash screen image with an arbitrary size. When sent repeatedly with different, large dimensions to a Jellyfin server, the requests will bypass caching and cause the server to generate multiple very large images, potentially impacting available disk space, memory, and CPU. With enough requests this can cause the target server to hang or crash.

At this point there is no known possibility of code execution or other similar effects beyond slowdowns and potential crashes.

### Patches
This issue has been fixed in versions 10.10.8 and the upcoming 10.11.0 (rc3 and newer).

### Workarounds
Block access to the `/Branding/Splashscreen` endpoint in your reverse proxy.

### References
N/A
